name: Pollyanna principle
statement: The words people use most often skew positive in every language yet measured, and the same preference is claimed for memory and perception on much thinner evidence.
meaning: Three separate claims travel under one name. The first is about word use: across a language's most frequent words, positive ones outnumber and outweigh negative ones. The second is about processing: pleasant material is recognised faster and judged more readily. The third is about memory: pleasant events and pleasant words are recalled better than unpleasant ones. Boucher and Osgood framed the first in 1969. Matlin and Stang's 1978 book extended the principle across all three, and its subtitle, selectivity in language, memory and thought, is the reason the three now get quoted together. The evidence behind them is not the same size. The word-use claim has been tested on hundreds of thousands of human ratings across ten languages. The memory claim rests on scattered laboratory work with results that depend on how the words were chosen.

origin.who: Jerry Boucher and Charles E. Osgood
origin.where: Journal of Verbal Learning and Verbal Behavior
origin.note: The paper "The Pollyanna hypothesis" runs from page 1 to page 8 of volume 8, issue 1. It is closed at the publisher, and Crossref, Unpaywall and OpenAlex list no open copy, so nothing is quoted from it here directly. Dodds and colleagues, who tested it, describe it as drawing on a selection of small-scale cross-cultural studies to argue that positive words are more prevalent, more meaningful, more diversely used and more readily learned, and judge that its findings "could only be regarded as suggestive". Matlin and Stang's 226-page book of 1978, published by Schenkman in Cambridge, Massachusetts, is the fullest statement of the wider principle. It was not obtained either, and no figure from it appears on this page.

evidence: The modern test is Dodds and thirteen colleagues, in 2015. They built 24 corpora across ten languages: English, Spanish, French, German, Brazilian Portuguese, Korean, Simplified Chinese, Russian, Indonesian and Arabic. Sources ran from Google Books and the Google Web Crawl to Twitter, the New York Times, music lyrics and film and television subtitles. From each corpus they took between 5,000 and 10,000 of the most frequently used words, aiming at about 10,000 per language and roughly 100,000 in all. Native speakers rated each word on a nine-point scale where 1 was saddest, 5 neutral and 9 happiest. Every word drew 50 ratings, for around 5 million individual assessments, from between 109 and 384 raters per language. For all 24 corpora the median sat above the neutral score of 5. Fitting average happiness against usage rank gives intercepts from 6.10 for the Spanish Google Web Crawl down to 5.21 for Chinese Google Books. The same fits are what the frequency claim rests on: Pearson correlations between a word's average happiness and its usage rank run from -0.187 for Korean film subtitles to +0.030 for Russian Google Books, with only that last one positive. The authors put the slope at about -1 in 100,000 per rank, which they gloss as happiness falling 0.1 over 10,000 words. Word scores also survived translation. Across all 45 language pairs, Pearson correlations for translation-stable words fell between 0.73 and 0.89, every p below 10 to the minus 118.

replication.headline: Independent corpora and a different sentiment instrument find the same above-neutral skew, while the claims that it is universal and independent of word frequency were both contested in the same journal.
replication.detail: Jacobs, Herrmann, Lauer, Lüdtke and Schroeder ran a different tool, SentiArt, over children's and youth literature in two languages. In 372 English books the mean affective-aesthetic potential was 0.29 with a standard error of 0.007 and the ratio of positive to negative words per sentence was 2.3, standard error 0.03; one book in the set came out negative overall. In 500 German books the mean was 0.06, standard error 0.004, above zero at z = 14.0, p < 0.0001, with a ratio of 1.5 and about 30% of books negative. Zhan and Jin applied sentiment and emotion analysis to doctors' narratives of patient deaths and split the result: positivity at the level of tokens, weak negativity at the level of types, positivity again at the level of whole texts. The largest counterweight is historical. Iliev, Hoover, Dehghani and Axelrod measured linguistic positivity across 192 billion words of Google Books from 1800 to 2000 and 14.9 million New York Times articles from 1851 to 2015. Positivity fell over the period, beta = -0.83, 95% CI [-0.91, -0.76], t(199) = -21.18, p < 0.001 in Google Books, and it tracked circumstance: war casualties at beta = -0.14 and -0.45 in the two corpora, an economic misery index at -0.35 and -0.42, and survey measures of subjective happiness at +0.33 and +0.31. The method dispute is separate. Garcia, Garas and Schweitzer reanalysed the English ratings against Warriner and Kuperman's larger lexicon and argued the bias is partly an artefact of the survey. LIWC's 399 function words, which should be emotionally neutral, took a median of 5.25 in the Dodds ratings, Wilcoxon p < 10 to the minus 11. The whole Dodds lexicon sat 0.28 above the reference lexicon in median happiness, and 0.07 above it on the 4,502 words the two share, t test p < 10 to the minus 15. Regressing happiness on log frequency rather than rank, they found a slope in four of six languages, with English happiness rising 1.06 across the frequency range. Dodds and colleagues replied that LIWC function words are not neutral, listing "greatest" at 7.26 and "worst" at 2.10 among them, and that regression on log frequency is improper because the word list thins out at low frequencies. On the shared-word scatter they report reduced major axis slopes of 1.04 for Warriner and Kuperman against their own data and 1.08 for the older ANEW list, and they note that ANEW's median of 5.29 falls below Warriner and Kuperman's 5.44, which is the wrong way round for the cartoon-face explanation. They also restate their own claim as "strongly" and "largely" independent of frequency rather than exactly independent.

study.cite: Iliev, R., Hoover, J., Dehghani, M., & Axelrod, R. (2016). Linguistic positivity in historical texts reflects dynamic environmental and psychological factors. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 113(49), E7871-E7879.

limits: Two founding documents were not read. Boucher and Osgood's paper is closed at Elsevier with no open copy indexed, and Matlin and Stang's book is available only on loan, so this page carries no number from either. What the 1969 paper actually measured is therefore described here at one remove, through Dodds and colleagues' summary of it. The memory claim has no equivalent to the 2015 word survey. Gomes, Brainerd and Stein tested it directly on 40 Brazilian undergraduates and found the Pollyanna pattern: by the third recall test, 71% of positive words were recalled against 65% of negative and 49% of neutral. A second experiment with 63 undergraduates crossed valence with arousal and the advantage narrowed, with positive recall beating negative only when arousal was high. That is the shape of the wider literature, where valence and arousal are routinely confounded and the confound decides the answer. Matlin and Gawron's 1979 note, two pages long, correlated 14 measures of Pollyannaism in 133 students and found they cohered with self-rated happiness, which is a claim about individual differences rather than about a general bias. No preregistered replication of the memory claim was located in searches of Crossref, Europe PMC, PubMed and OSF. On the language side, Dodds and colleagues acknowledge their instrument can fail on individual words through polysemy and language change, and their translation analysis used Google Translate rather than human translators.
misreadings: The word-use finding is not a finding about texts. Dodds and colleagues say so in the paper: their result "in no way asserts all natural texts will skew positive", and their own worked example shows Moby-Dick and Crime and Punishment both ending below neutral. The second error is letting the language evidence carry the memory claim. Five million ratings of 100,000 words say nothing about whether a person recalls a good day better than a bad one, and the studies that do ask give an answer that depends on arousal. The third is reading universal as constant. Every corpus Dodds sampled was above neutral, and Iliev and colleagues show the level moving with wars and economic conditions across two centuries. The fourth is treating frequency independence as exact. The 2015 paper's own tables give a small non-zero slope in every corpus and call the independence strong rather than complete, and the disagreement with Garcia and colleagues is about how large the departure is, not whether one exists. The last is the family confusion. The Pollyanna principle, rosy retrospection and the fading affect bias are three claims with three evidence bases, and only the first is about which words a language uses most.
